name: PT Pancaran Samudera Transport Tbk

frontmatter.title: Pancaran Samudera Transport - a coal hauler whose multiple does not survive the replacement cost
frontmatter.summary: PSAT moves coal, nickel and bauxite on a renewed domestic fleet. FY2025 growth came from related-party goods trading, not the owned ships; H1 2026 shows the owned fleet growing while the group shrinks. Once sustaining capex is anchored to the fleet's replacement cost, the DCF sits below the price, and the peer multiples that carried the initiation are not justified by the company's return on equity. We move to REDUCE.
thesis: PSAT is a domestic volume-and-spread shipper, not a miner: barges, tugs and bulk carriers earn a freight rate per voyage, so utilisation, the owned-versus-chartered mix and fleet replacement drive the value [S15, S19].

FY2025's growth was not the core fleet: related-party revenue rose from a base while third-party revenue was flat, and goods trading became a fifth of the book. H1 2026 reverses the mix, with owned-vessel revenue up nearly a fifth and the re-charter book down more than a third [S15, S14].

The fleet was renewed with IPO money and is young, but a going concern must replace it: vessels of IDR1,429.4bn gross, docking assets of IDR122.5bn and lives of 16.0 to twenty years put sustaining capex at 17.0% of revenue, not the low single-digit rate the initiation assumed [S15 note 10].

Tax includes a final levy of IDR9.1bn on shipping revenue plus the corporate rate on non-shipping profit, so the effective rate was low in the strong FY2024 year and high on FY2025's thin profit; the forecast carries the effective rate, not a flat charge [S15 note 28].
The DCF at a 12.5% cost of capital is Rp535, below the Rp845 price; the EV/EBITDA cross-check is the only method above it, and it is struck on trough trailing EBITDA [S0].

June liquidity is thin: cash of IDR12.0bn against current liabilities of IDR227.7bn and bank and lease debt of IDR13.5bn, IDR27.6bn, IDR102.3bn, IDR11.5bn and IDR20.3bn; the first-half repayment came from the cash balance, not free cash flow [S14].

blocks.text: **Rating: REDUCE · target Rp708 · last close Rp845 · return -15.1%**

We are changing the call from BUY to REDUCE. The operating story is intact and in one respect better than we first wrote it: the owned fleet is growing while the low-margin book shrinks, and the first half of 2026 was a cleaner business than the transition year. What does not survive the red team's audit is the valuation construction. The initiation valued PSAT on a DCF whose terminal cash flow added back far more depreciation than it spent on replacement vessels, and then lifted the answer with peer multiples that the company's own return on equity does not support. Corrected, the DCF is Rp535 against a Rp845 price, and the probability-weighted target after the liquidity discount is Rp708, a return of -15.1% [S15, S14].

The three corrections are worth stating plainly. First, sustaining capex is now anchored to the assets the LK describes, not to a percentage of revenue: vessels at IDR1,429.4bn gross depreciating over 16.0 to twenty years, docking assets of IDR122.5bn amortised at 40.0%, and the rest of the fixed-asset base. That is a replacement charge of about 17.0% of revenue, and it holds through the terminal value; a fleet that grows in perpetuity must be replaced, not run down [S15 note 10]. Second, the gross margin holds the first-half cash margin after allowing for the deck's higher Brent, rather than assuming an unsourced second-half squeeze: the key input is 19.5% before the bunker link, and the link then deducts the unpassed quarter against the deck's US$96.0 Brent, so the printed FY2026E gross margin is 18.5% and EBITDA is IDR237.3bn [S14, S0]. Third, tax is rebuilt from the LK's final levy on shipping revenue plus the corporate rate on the non-shipping business; the effective rate is 23.0% in FY2026E and fades to 15.0%, because the final levy is revenue-based and does not rise with margin [S15 note 28]. The volume backdrop is not a tailwind: the revised 2026 coal quota of 700 Mt is below the 817 Mt actually produced in 2025, and it is a national target rather than a miner-level allocation or a PSAT freight contract, so the base case assumes no second-half cargo uplift [S23].

The result is a valuation that is no longer supported by the cross-checks. The DCF is Rp535, with the terminal value at 48.7% of enterprise value, so it is not a terminal artefact. The EV/EBITDA cross-check applies the peer median of 12.9x to trailing EBITDA and gives Rp1,588, 196.7% above the DCF; we keep it at a 15.0% weight as a cross-check, not a value [S0]. The P/BV cross-check is gone. At a sustainable return on equity of 4.7%, a cost of equity of 13.2% and terminal growth of 4.0%, the Gordon-consistent P/B is (ROE less growth) over (cost of equity less growth), which is below one times book, not the peer median the engine carried [S0, S15].

The variant view has therefore flipped. We do not think the market is wrong about the business; we think it is paying a multiple that requires a margin recovery to the FY2024 structure, when the cash gross margin was near its peak and the re-charter book was small. Our base case holds the first-half cash margin and a partial mix repair, and still gets a value below the price. What would change our mind is evidence that the owned fleet can keep growing without the re-charter book returning: a second half in which owned-vessel revenue rises again while the group gross margin holds would move us back toward the base case, and a dividend at the stated ceiling would compress the liquidity discount. That is the signpost to watch, not the coal price [S14, S19].

The bear and bull cases bracket the base with mirrored shocks. All three scenario targets are stated before the liquidity discount: the bear gives Rp439, the base Rp776 and the bull Rp1,550, and the probability-weighted value is Rp885 [S0]. The bull is doing a lot of work in the weighted number, which is exactly why we state the base-case target alongside it. With the bull set equal to the base, the probability-weighted value before the discount would be the base-case number; the call does not need the bull to be a REDUCE.

Indonesian coal logistics is a domestic freight business layered on a policy-driven mining cycle. Miners produce the coal; barge operators move it from mine jetties to power plants, cement works and transhipment anchorages. The barriers are vessels, permits, customer relationships and working capital rather than geology, and operators compete for annual cargo allocations from a small number of large miners and the state utility. Revenue is a freight rate per tonne or per voyage, so utilisation and the owned-versus-rented mix matter more than the coal price itself.

PT Pancaran Samudera Transport was founded in April 2007 in Jakarta and listed on the Indonesia Stock Exchange in July 2025 as a coal-distribution name under the energy sector [S7, S11]. It operates two businesses: a shipping division that moves bulk cargoes, mainly coal, on its own and chartered-in vessels, and a shipyard division that repairs and builds vessels through PT Pancaran Samudera Shipyard; vessel ownership sits in PT Pancaran Karya Shipping, the subsidiary that received most of the IPO proceeds [S19, S10]. The group employed 240.0 people at the last count [S0].

The operating fleet at the end of 2025 was 30.0 count barges, 35.0 count tugboats and a small group of bulk carriers, after a renewal programme in which four elderly vessels were sold for IDR22.0bn in July 2025 and two bulk carriers were bought from an affiliate with IPO money [S19, S7, S10]. The barges and tugs serve the domestic coal trade from Kalimantan and Sumatra to the Java and Bali power stations, cement plants and industrial sites; the company also runs port-to-ship and ship-to-ship transfers for the larger export-bound mother vessels [S2]. The bulk carriers extend the range to nickel and bauxite cargoes, the diversification management has flagged for 2026 [S19].

Revenue splits between owned-vessel freight, re-chartered freight, sales of goods and docking services. In FY2025 owned-vessel freight from third parties was IDR448.4bn, the re-charter book was IDR358.1bn, and docking services were small; sales of goods were IDR86.3bn to related parties and IDR139.7bn to third parties, a goods book of about a fifth of group revenue of which more than a third was related-party [S15 note 21]. The shipping segment produced IDR815.3bn of revenue and most of the gross profit, while the shipyard added IDR296.9bn of revenue and a smaller, steadier contribution [S15]. No gross margin is disclosed for the goods line, and we do not invent one; the absence is itself a disclosure gap, and the line is the channel through which FY2025 growth arrived [S15].

H1 2026 shows the mix reversing. Total revenue fell to IDR434.6bn from a much higher first half, but owned-vessel revenue from third parties rose to IDR252.5bn from the prior-year third-party owned line, and related-party owned-vessel revenue added IDR2.2bn [S14 note 22]. The re-charter book fell to IDR127.6bn, goods sales to IDR35.9bn plus IDR12.9bn, and docking revenue to IDR2.8bn plus IDR0.6bn [S14]. The decline is therefore concentrated in the low-margin pass-through lines while the core owned fleet grew. That is the strongest operating fact in the file and it belongs in the bull case; the revenue path below is built from it [S14].

The customer list is concentrated but not single-customer. Three customers each took more than a tenth of FY2025 revenue: Kideco Jaya Agung at 17.5%, Vale Indonesia at 14.2% and Dian Ciptamas Agung at 10.9% [S15]. Kideco is a coal miner, Vale is a nickel producer, and Dian Ciptamas is a coal and minerals trader, so the book already spans more than one commodity [S15]. That is a meaningful difference from a pure coal barge operator, and it is the commercial foundation for the nickel and bauxite diversification.

Control is concentrated. PT Profitama Hasil Indah holds 60.4% and PT Surya Mitra Pancaran holds 24.6% after the IPO, leaving the balance in public hands [S11] and an IDX free float of 13.2% [S0]; the free-float measure is below the public holding because the exchange excludes the portions it treats as non-free. The two controlling shareholders are related to the founding family, and the group transacts with a list of affiliated companies in shipping, land transport, shipyards and logistics [S15]. Related-party revenue was IDR99.4bn in FY2025, mostly sales of goods, against a negligible base a year earlier; that jump is a governance fact the reader should hold alongside the operating story, and it is why related-party revenue and related-party goods are not treated as recurring third-party demand in the forecast [S15 note 21, note 31].

Management's strategy for 2026 is explicit: diversify the commodity mix beyond coal, widen the delivery footprint, add customers, digitise operations, tighten customer relationship management and improve governance [S19]. The company has already moved into nickel through the Vale relationship and is targeting bauxite and other bulk cargoes with the new bulk carriers [S19]. The strategy is sensible for a coal hauler facing a structural decline in domestic coal volumes; the risk is that it is executed with related-party assets and a thin public float.

The domestic coal logistics market is sized by the coal that is mined and moved, not by the seaborne price. Indonesia produced 817 Mt of coal in 2025, according to the energy ministry's revised figures, and the initial 2026 quota was set at 600 Mt before being revised up to 700 Mt in October 2026 [S23, S19]. The revision matters for PSAT because its barges and tugs are employed against mine output: every million tonnes of quota restored is a tranche of voyage demand, and the 154 Mt allocated to PLN power plants is the part of the market that moves on barges rather than capex-heavy export infrastructure [S23].

But the revision does not restore the 2025 book. The 700 Mt quota is below the 817 Mt actually produced in 2025, and it is a national target rather than a miner-level allocation or a PSAT freight contract [S23]. We therefore do not assume a second-half uplift: FY2026E revenue of IDR869.0bn holds the first-half run-rate, and the recovery starts in FY2027E at 6.0% [S14, S23]. The initiation's "restores cargoes" language overstated the revision; the base case now carries the gap explicitly. The bull case is where the late-October quota and the nickel and bauxite contracts do the work, and even there the shock is a growth shock, not a volume contract [S23, S19].

The coal deck we carry prices the seaborne market at US$137.0 a tonne for FY2026E, easing to US$118.0 and US$105.0 long run, against US$108.4 in FY2025 [S0]. Spot is US$150.3, above the forward path, and the government cited a US$154.0 print for 6,330 kcal coal in October 2026 when it decided to relax the quota [S23]. The domestic price cap for power-station coal is US$70.0 a tonne, and the HBA reference for FY2027E is US$112.0 [S0]. For PSAT the coal price is a demand and freight-rate signal, not a cost: it buys no coal, and its cost of revenue is charter-in, fuel, subcontractors, depreciation, port charges and crew [S15]. That is why the engine's coal cost link is set to zero and the deck enters the model only through the revenue-growth path and the scenarios; a reader looking for a coal-price sensitivity in cost of revenue will not find one, because there is none [S15].

Fuel is the direct commodity exposure. Brent averaged US$68.1 a barrel in FY2025 and the deck carries US$96.0 for FY2026E, easing to US$84.0 and US$75.0 long run; spot is US$117.6 [S0]. Bunker was IDR111.8bn of FY2025 cost of revenue, about an eighth of the total, and the company can recover most of a fuel move through freight rates with a lag [S15]. The FY2025 margin collapse was not a fuel story: bunker cost rose only slightly while short-term charter cost more than doubled, which is a mix and fleet-availability problem rather than an oil-price problem [S15].

Regulation reaches the business through three channels. The annual RKAB quota sets how much coal the miners may produce and therefore how much cargo exists; the DMO sets the share that must go to the domestic market, including the 154 Mt reserved for PLN in 2026; and export-proceeds rules and royalty changes alter the miners' incentive to produce for export versus domestic consumption [S23, S19]. For a domestic barge operator the DMO is the friendlier part of the regime, because it keeps a floor under power-station coal movements even when export prices fall.

Competition is fragmented at the barge-owner level and consolidated at the customer level. The listed peer set includes ALII, BBRM, BESS, DWGL and SGER, each with a different mix of barging, trading and port services; PSAT is a mid-sized challenger with a shipyard attached rather than a market leader [S0, S15]. Barriers are vessels, permits and relationships, not technology; a well-capitalised operator can add capacity, which is why freight rates cycle. PSAT's differentiation is the combination of owned barges, bulk carriers and a repair yard, which lets it keep utilisation up when cargoes are thin and repair its own fleet; its weakness is that the customer base is a handful of miners and the contracts re-price.

The five forces are mixed. Buyer power is high: three customers take more than a tenth of revenue each and the miners can switch barge operators [S15]. Supplier power is moderate: charter-in vessels are available, but rates spike when the fleet is tight, as FY2025 showed [S15]. New entrants are a constant threat in barging, though the capital cost of tugs and barges and the permit requirements raise the hurdle. Substitutes are pipeline and rail in the very long run, but road and barge remain the practical route for most domestic coal. Rivalry is high on price and utilisation. Industry returns therefore depend on fleet positioning and contract discipline, which is what the FY2025 mix shift tested.

Revenue grew from IDR811.4bn in FY2022 to IDR980.2bn in FY2024, then rose 9.9% to IDR1,076.8bn in FY2025 [S0, S15]. The FY2025 increase was not a good-news year: owned-vessel freight revenue fell to IDR448.4bn from IDR620.2bn, the re-charter book rose to IDR358.1bn from IDR199.7bn, and sales of goods and docking fees filled the gap [S15]. The related-party note shows where the growth came from: related-party revenue rose to IDR99.4bn while third-party revenue was flat, and goods trading reached IDR86.3bn plus IDR139.7bn [S15 note 21]. Stripping the goods line out, the freight and docking business did not grow in FY2025; the group did. The revenue path below is therefore built from the H1 2026 line mix rather than extrapolated from the FY2025 total [S14, S15].

The margin is the story, and it needs a bridge because the reported gross margin is struck after the vessel depreciation inside cost of revenue. Reported gross margin fell from 33.4% in FY2024 to 13.5% in FY2025, and net margin from 24.8% to 2.1% [S0, S15]. The cost note makes the cause explicit: short-term chartered-in vessel cost rose to IDR273.6bn from IDR126.9bn, materials and subcontractor services rose to IDR225.4bn from IDR111.1bn, while bunker was broadly flat at IDR111.8bn [S15]. Re-chartered voyages are a low-margin pass-through: PSAT rents a vessel, resells the voyage and keeps a thin spread, so a doubling of that book adds revenue and almost no gross profit.

The cash margin does not tell the same stability story the initiation told. Adding total depreciation back, the FY2025 cash gross margin is gross profit of IDR145.8bn plus depreciation of IDR156.9bn on revenue of IDR1,076.8bn; FY2024 is IDR327.3bn plus IDR133.1bn on IDR980.2bn. The annual cash margin fell with the re-charter mix, by roughly the same order as the reported margin, so the claim that the underlying cash margin is "far more stable" was wrong on the annual numbers. What is stable is the first-half pair: H1 2026 gross profit of IDR82.9bn plus depreciation of IDR82.9bn and IDR10.9bn on revenue of IDR434.6bn is close to the prior first half, even though reported revenue fell [S14]. We present the build rather than a single ratio because the prior draft's H1 figure did not reproduce [S14, S15].

A restatement is still needed before any margin work. The data pack carries FY2025 D&A of a few billion rupiah, but the accounts show total depreciation of IDR156.9bn, split between fixed assets of IDR135.6bn and right-of-use vessels of IDR21.3bn, and FY2024 of IDR133.1bn [S15, S16]. The pack's figure is a fraction of the real charge because the Indonesian cash-flow statement reports depreciation only inside the notes; the model uses the filing's total, which is why EBITDA in this report is IDR195.0bn rather than the pack's much smaller figure [S15]. The reported EBIT of IDR38.1bn is unchanged; only the add-back is corrected. H1 2026 fixed-asset depreciation of IDR82.9bn plus right-of-use depreciation of IDR10.9bn annualises to about IDR186.8bn, which is the charge the forecast carries [S14].

H1 2026 is the first clean read on the post-transition business. Revenue was IDR434.6bn, gross profit IDR82.9bn and net profit IDR14.8bn [S14]. The revenue decline is the coal-volume cut and the collapse of the low-margin re-charter, goods and docking lines; the margin repair is the mix moving back to owned vessels, whose third-party revenue rose to IDR252.5bn [S14, S19]. The owned fleet is therefore earning a normal freight spread on a smaller book, and the group margin is being held down by the depreciation of a fleet that is already in service, not by a cash-margin squeeze [S14].

Our forecast reproduces the H1 run-rate rather than the FY2025 trough. FY2026E revenue falls -19.3% to IDR869.0bn, gross margin is 18.5%, and EBITDA is IDR237.3bn at a 27.3% margin against 18.1% in FY2025 [S14, S15]. The key input is 19.5% before the bunker link; the engine then deducts the unpassed quarter of the deck's higher Brent (US$96.0 for FY2026E against US$68.1 in FY2025), which is why the printed margin sits just below the H1 2026 reported level and the cash margin is close to, not above, the H1 figure [S14, S0]. The FY2025 to FY2026 EBITDA bridge is a mix and depreciation step, not a cash-margin step: the gross margin adds as the re-charter book shrinks, the depreciation add-back adds because the new bulk carriers are in service on a smaller revenue base, and the SG&A ratio subtracts as fixed costs meet the smaller book [S14 note 22, S15 note 10]. The FY2026E margin is below the H1 2026 actual, so the model does not assume a margin gain; the QC record carries the like-for-like justification [S14]. Net profit is only IDR27.9bn because the depreciation charge is heavy and interest takes a large share of what remains of operating profit; the cash flow is the better measure of the business [S15].

Depreciation and capex are the heart of the revision. The LK's fixed-asset note gives vessels of IDR1,429.4bn gross depreciating over 16.0 to twenty years, docking assets of IDR122.5bn amortised at 40.0%, and the rest of the fixed-asset base; the replacement charge is about 17.0% of revenue, and we hold it through FY2035E [S15 note 10]. The prior model spent below the replacement rate and let fixed assets run down to a fraction of book by the terminal year, which is not a going-concern steady state: a fleet that grows with the economy must be replaced, and the terminal value must not capitalise a depreciation add-back. Capex is lumpy: the first half ran at about IDR54.4bn against first-half revenue of IDR434.6bn, below the annual replacement charge because the docking cycle is uneven, so the model uses the annual average rather than the half-year print [S14]. FY2026E capex is IDR147.7bn and FCFF is IDR26.4bn, not the much larger number a below-replacement capex would produce [S15, S14].

Cash flow is what supports the valuation, and it is thinner than the initiation suggested. FY2025 operating cash flow was IDR156.6bn, positive despite the profit collapse, because depreciation is large; capex was IDR442.2bn, the fleet-renewal year, which is why free cash flow was negative [S15]. H1 2026 operating cash flow was IDR57.7bn and capex IDR54.4bn, leaving a small free-cash balance before the debt repayment [S14]. The company is not a cash compounder yet; it is a capital-intensive operator whose cash flow depends on the replacement cycle and on collecting from miners.

Working capital is a live risk and the inventory line is the new fact. FY2025 operating working capital was IDR303.0bn, a little over a quarter of revenue; at June 2026 inventories had risen to IDR266.5bn from the December level, while current liabilities were IDR227.7bn [S15, S14]. The receivables book is short and the customer base is large miners, which is a comfort; the counterparty risk is the related-party balances and the sales advances [S15]. We hold working capital at the 30 June 2026 actual of 40.8% of revenue through the forecast, rather than assuming a release; there is no disclosed terms-of-trade improvement or customer-payment change to support a fade [S15, S14]. A shipping company does not need a large inventory unless it is carrying trading stock, and the goods-trading line is the related-party channel; that is why the inventory build is a governance and liquidity item, not just a working-capital item [S14].

The June balance sheet is the liquidity fact the initiation missed. Cash was IDR12.0bn at 30 June 2026, down from IDR66.6bn at December 2025, against short-term bank loans of IDR13.5bn, bank loans due within a year of IDR27.6bn, long-term bank loans of IDR102.3bn and lease liabilities of IDR11.5bn and IDR20.3bn [S14 p5-7]. H1 operating cash flow of IDR57.7bn less capex of IDR54.4bn leaves a small free-cash balance before the net bank repayment and the lease payments, which were funded by drawing down cash rather than by free cash flow [S14 p8]. Current assets still cover current liabilities, but the headroom is thinner than the December accounts suggested, and the first-half interest paid of IDR6.7bn is already inside operating cash flow [S14]. The forecast charges interest on the December 2025 opening debt rather than the average of the December and June balances, so the FY2026E charge is marginally conservative and NP and DPS are if anything understated; the FY2027E charge falls with the repaid balance [S14]. Net debt/EBITDA is 0.6x times in FY2026E and the debt is bank facilities plus leases rather than a bond, but the liquidity buffer is the constraint to watch [S15, S14]. The IPO proceeds of IDR193.3bn net of costs were fully deployed by the June 2026 public expose, so there is no unspent cash cushion left [S19, S9].

Capital allocation is the weak point, and the dividend is the anchor the sector uses. The company paid IDR100.0bn of dividends in FY2025, but that was declared at the March 2025 AGM before the IPO and paid to the pre-IPO shareholders; at the June 2026 AGM the board skipped a FY2025 dividend entirely, despite a prospectus policy of up to 100.0% of net profit from FY2026 [S15, S10, S17]. The skipped payment was a capex decision on a prior year, not a policy for FY2026; with the fleet renewed and capex now at replacement, we model a 50.0% payout from FY2026 earnings, paid the following year, half the stated ceiling [S10, S17]. The capacity is real but modest: FY2028E EPS of Rp44 at the full stated payout would distribute that amount, against the modelled Rp22 at the half payout, and the FCFE yield is 5.2% at the modelled payout [S0]. A dividend yield of 2.6% on the current price is the anchor, not a growth multiple [S0].

The earnings-quality screens are mixed but not disqualifying. Accruals are not the problem: operating cash flow exceeded net profit in FY2025 and H1 2026 because of depreciation [S15, S14]. The divergence is in related-party flows: related-party revenue of IDR99.4bn in FY2025, almost all of it sales of goods, from a negligible base, and there are related-party sales advances and other payables on the balance sheet [S15]. Receivables and contract assets grew faster than revenue into H1 2026, and inventories rose to IDR266.5bn, which we hold at the last actual rather than dismiss [S14]. We found no evidence of a special-monitoring board or notation status in the filings, but we could not verify the exchange's current notation from a primary announcement in this window, so we do not claim one [S15].

We value PSAT primarily on a discounted cash flow of free cash flow to the firm, because the company owns a finite fleet that earns a freight spread, and the value is the present value of the voyages that fleet can make, not a multiple of a cycle-peak profit [S15]. The industry method set blends the DCF with an EV/EBITDA cross-check; we weight the DCF at 85.0% and the cross-check at 15.0% [S0]. The P/BV cross-check is dropped. The peer median is carried at more than one and a half times book, but the modelled return on equity is 4.7% in FY2028E and below the cost of equity through the forecast, so the Gordon-consistent P/B is (ROE less growth) over (cost of equity less growth): at 4.7%, 13.2% and 4.0% that is below one times book. Applying a peer P/B to a company that does not earn its cost of equity would import the peer's overvaluation, which is the error we are trying to avoid [S0, S15].

The cost of capital is a rupiah build, and the build must show the default-spread adjustment. The risk-free rate is the ten-year Indonesian government yield of 7.4%; because that yield embeds the sovereign default risk that the country premium also carries, we deduct the 1.6% default spread to reach the rupiah risk-free-equivalent [S0]. We then apply a levered beta of 1.11 to the mature-market equity risk premium of 4.2% plus the country risk premium of 2.5%, which gives a cost of equity of 13.2% [S0]. Debt costs 9.4% pre-tax and is 12.3% of the capital structure at the 22.0% tax rate, with equity at 87.7%, so the WACC is 12.5% [S0]. Terminal growth is the house rupiah rate of 4.0%, appropriate for a domestic freight business that grows with the economy rather than with the coal price [S19]. The bull scenario's lower WACC is now half a percentage point below the base, not the two-point cut that took it below every peer; the bear mirrors it, so the scenario construction stays symmetric [S0].

The DCF produces Rp535, with the terminal value at 48.7% of enterprise value, so it is not a terminal-value artefact [S0]. The cash flows that support it are ordinary: revenue recovering modestly from the FY2026 trough, the cash gross margin holding at the first-half rate, capex at the fleet replacement charge and working capital held at the last actual [S15, S14]. The valuation is most sensitive to the gross margin and to the capex ratio, as the sensitivity table shows; those are the two assumptions we would revisit first if the second-half results differ [S0].

The EV/EBITDA cross-check is the only method that diverges sharply, and it diverges upward: 12.9x times trailing EBITDA gives Rp1,588, 196.7% above the DCF [S0]. That is a cross-check, not a value. The peer set mixes barging operators trading at low-single-digit EV/EBITDA with traders and producers at multiples of that, so the median is not a benchmark for a volume-and-spread hauler; PSAT itself trades at 5.9x forward EBITDA [S0]. The engine also applies the multiple to trailing EBITDA, which is the FY2025 trough; on FY2026E EBITDA of IDR237.3bn the same multiple would be higher still, which is another reason not to capitalise it at full weight [S0]. We keep it at 15.0% so the reader can see the gap, and the gap is the story: the market is pricing the peer multiple, not the cash flows [S0].

The weighted value is Rp885 before the liquidity discount and Rp708 after it; the discount is 20.0%, reflecting a three-month traded value of IDR0.1bn a day against a market capitalisation of IDR1,252.6bn and a free float of 13.2% [S0]. It is not a governance judgement; it reflects the fact that a position cannot be built or exited at the quoted price [S0]. The base-case target before the discount is Rp776; the bull target is Rp1,550 and the bear Rp439 [S0]. The bull contributes the difference between the base and the weighted number, and with the bull set equal to the base the weighted answer is the base-case target. We say that plainly because the initiation's return depended on the bull and on the multiple convergence [S0].

What does today's price imply? The reverse DCF cannot bracket the price on revenue growth alone: even the top of the growth grid does not reach Rp845, which means the market is paying for a gross margin or a cost of capital outside our base-case grid [S0]. The price sits between the DCF and the peer multiple, and the gap to the DCF is the part of the return the initiation attributed to multiple convergence. We do not think a controlled, thinly traded company with a related-party goods book should converge to the peer median, and the P/BV analysis says the same thing from the balance sheet: at the modelled return on equity, book value does not support the peer multiple [S0, S15].

The bear case is a volume, mix and liquidity story. It assumes the revised quota does not restore cargoes quickly, a top-three customer re-tenders its book away, the re-charter book returns with its thin spread, and the market keeps a governance discount for the related-party goods book and the thin free float [S15, S23]. The shocks are mirrored with the bull at the same size: revenue growth and gross margin move by the same amount in opposite directions, and the cost of capital moves by the same amount in opposite directions [S0]. The bear gives Rp439 before the liquidity discount, above zero because the owned fleet and the shipyard have value and the balance sheet does not force a dilution; a bear that reached zero would need a fleet write-down and a covenant breach, neither of which the filings support [S15].

The bull case is the mirror. The quota revision lifts late-year cargoes, the owned-vessel revenue that grew in H1 2026 keeps compounding as the bulk carriers win nickel and bauxite business, fuel costs ease with Brent, and a first post-IPO dividend at the stated payout begins to close the governance gap [S23, S19, S10]. It gives Rp1,550 before the liquidity discount. Both branches use the same three levers, and the probabilities are 25.0% bear, 50.0% base and 25.0% bull [S0].

| Risk | Likelihood | Impact | What we watch | |---|---|---|---| | Coal volume — the revised quota is below 2025 output | High | High | Monthly RKAB quota, mine production and barge utilisation [S23, S19] | | Customer concentration — three customers above a tenth of revenue | High | High | Contract renewals at Kideco, Vale and Dian Ciptamas [S15] | | Mix — a return to low-margin re-chartered tonnage | Medium | High | Owned versus re-chartered revenue in each quarterly filing [S15, S14] | | Related-party goods trading — inventory and receivable build | Medium | High | The goods line, inventory and related-party sales advances [S15, S14] | | Balance-sheet liquidity — cash against current liabilities and maturities | High | High | Cash, current liabilities and the bank-facility covenant position [S14] | | Fuel — Brent above the deck path squeezes the unpassed quarter | Medium | Medium | Bunker cost and the gross margin in the H2 results [S15] | | Governance — related-party fleet purchases and a thin free float | Medium | High | Any new affiliate asset purchase or related-party receivable [S15, S10] | | Liquidity — daily traded value is tiny relative to market capitalisation | High | Medium | Traded value and the free float in each quarterly filing [S0] | | Capital allocation — capex and dividends compete for the same cash | Medium | Medium | Capex guidance and the FY2026 AGM dividend decision [S14, S17] | | Energy transition — thermal coal demand declines beyond the horizon | Low within the horizon | High beyond it | National coal output and PLN's generation mix [S23] |

The signposts that would change our view: a second half in which owned-vessel revenue keeps rising while the re-charter book shrinks would confirm the mix repair and move us toward the base case; a new related-party asset purchase above independent appraisal would say the governance discount is warranted; a dividend at the stated ceiling would signal that the board is willing to share cash and would compress the liquidity discount; and a 2027 coal quota below the revised 2026 level would make the volume recovery a one-year event [S15, S19, S23]. The liquidity signpost is now as important as the volume one: a further drawdown of cash against current liabilities would make the equity value sensitive to the debt maturity schedule [S14].

Ownership is the first governance fact. PT Profitama Hasil Indah holds 60.4% and PT Surya Mitra Pancaran holds 24.6% after the IPO, the public holds the balance [S11], and the IDX free float of 13.2% is thin enough that the price is set by a small number of holders [S0]. The controlling shareholders are related to the founding family. We found no disclosure of pledged controlling shares in the annual or interim accounts, and we checked the balance-sheet and equity notes; that is an absence of evidence, not proof, and it belongs on the watch list [S15].

Related-party gravity is the main issue, and it is now quantified rather than waved at. Related-party revenue was IDR99.4bn in FY2025, of which IDR86.3bn was sales of goods, against almost nothing a year earlier [S15]. Goods trading was a fifth of group revenue, and more than a third of it was related-party; the counterparties behind the related-party sales are disclosed in the related-party note but the margin on the line is not [S15 note 21, note 31]. The company also buys vessels from an affiliate, PT Pancaran Maritim Transportindo: the two bulk carriers bought with IPO proceeds came from that related party under a February 2025 agreement, at a price set by an independent appraiser [S10, S11]. The transaction is disclosed and independently valued, so it is optics-class rather than manipulation-class, but a controlling family selling vessels to a listed company is exactly the channel through which value leaks on this exchange, and the related-party goods book shows the channel is active [S10, S15].

The board is small and family-linked. The president director is Susanto, the finance director is Wendi Arifin and the corporate secretary is Fadzil Fahreza; Olivia Djoharsjah is president commissioner [S0, S19]. There is no large independent shareholder of record, and the public float is thin enough that minority holders cannot easily challenge a related-party resolution [S0, S11]. We could not read the auditor's opinion from the archived scan of the FY2025 report; the accounts were audited and filed, but the opinion page is an image, so we make no claim about the opinion beyond its inclusion [S15].

The dividend record is a credibility issue. The prospectus promised a payout of up to 100.0% of net profit from FY2026, but the board skipped the FY2025 dividend at the June 2026 AGM to retain capital for fleet capacity [S10, S17]. That is within the board's discretion, but it is a clear choice of retention over distribution, and it weakens the dividend anchor that investors usually rely on in this sector [S15, S17]. We model a 50.0% payout, half the stated ceiling, and we show the capacity to pay more; the first real test is the FY2026 AGM [S10, S17].

On ESG, the exposures are those of a coal and mineral carrier: emissions from the cargo it moves, fuel consumption and spills from the fleet, labour and safety conditions on barges and at the shipyard, and the transition risk of its coal customers [S19]. The company describes safety and environmental programmes in its public materials but does not quantify them [S19]. We do not treat ESG as a separate valuation driver within the horizon; it is a slow erosion of terminal value, and the terminal growth rate reflects that rather than a discrete haircut.

The near catalyst is the nine-month 2026 results, which the company has not yet posted on its investor site. They will show whether the H1 mix repair held through the third quarter, when the coal quota was still tight, and whether the revised RKAB quota began to lift voyage demand late in the period [S19, S23]. We will compare the owned-versus-re-chartered revenue split, the gross margin and the contract-asset balance against the H1 figures.

The next catalyst is the FY2026 audited result and the AGM early in 2027, which will settle the dividend question after the skipped FY2025 payment [S17]. A dividend at or near the promised payout would be read as a governance positive; another year of retention would reinforce the discount.

The structural catalyst is the 2027 RKAB quota and the nickel and bauxite contracts. The revised 2026 quota of 700 Mt with 154 Mt for PLN is the base for the volume recovery; a 2027 quota at or above that level would make the recovery durable, while a cut would make it a one-year bounce [S23]. The bulk-carrier fleet and the Vale relationship are the seed of the nickel business, and the first meaningful non-coal tonnage would reduce the coal beta that the market currently applies [S19, S15].

Between updates we monitor five numbers: the owned-to-re-chartered revenue ratio, which drives the gross margin; the related-party goods line and the inventory balance, which are the governance and liquidity channel; cash against current liabilities and debt maturities; capex against the replacement charge; and the daily traded value against the free float, which sets the size of the liquidity discount [S15, S14, S0]. We will also watch the coal deck's Newcastle and HBA paths and Brent, because they set the demand and fuel backdrop even though PSAT does not sell coal [S0].

sensitivity.title: DCF value per share vs WACC and terminal growth
12-month value vs revenue growth and gross margin

assumptions.label: Revenue growth
assumptions.basis: H1 2026 revenue was Rp434.6bn, 20.4% below H1 2025 (Rp545.9bn), on a coal-volume cut. FY2026E holds H2 flat to H1 (H1 x2 = Rp869.1bn, -19.3% on FY2025): the October 2026 revision of the 2026 RKAB quota to 700Mt is 14.4% below the 817.5Mt actually produced in 2025 and is a national target, not a PSAT jetty allocation, so no H2 h/h uplift is sourced [S14, S23, F32, F33]. FY2027E +6% is built from the H1 line mix: owned-vessel revenue grew 16.9% in H1 2026 to Rp254.7bn (Rp509bn annualised) while re-charter fell 41%, so a 10% owned-fleet recovery plus a flat re-charter and goods book carries the group; growth fades to the house rupiah rate [S14, S23].

assumptions.label: Gross margin (reported, after D&A in cost of revenue)
assumptions.basis: The LK puts vessel depreciation inside cost of revenue, so the reported gross margin is the right input and D&A is added back to reach EBITDA. FY2025 reported 13.5% (revenue Rp1,076.8bn, gross profit Rp145.8bn) was the transition-year trough; H1 2026 recovered to 19.1% (Rp82.9bn on Rp434.6bn) as the mix shifted back to owned vessels and the low-margin re-charter book shrank 41% [S15, S14]. The input is stated before the engine's bunker link: we set 19.5%, a touch above the H1 reported margin, and the link then deducts the unpassed quarter against the deck's FY2026E Brent (US$96.0 against US$68.1 in FY2025), so the printed FY2026E gross margin is 18.5% and the cash margin is 40.0% against the 40.7% H1 actual [S14, S0]. We let the reported margin rise only as the D&A ratio falls with revenue recovery (21.5% to 17%); it climbs from the printed 18.5% to 23.5%, still well below the FY2024 33.4% peak. There is no sourced reason for an H2 cash-margin squeeze below the H1 actual [S14, S15].

assumptions.label: Cost link 1: share of COGS exposed
assumptions.basis: No coal purchase line exists in the cost stack: FY2025 cost of revenue is short-term charter (29.4%), materials and subcontractor services (24.2%), depreciation (14.3%), bunker (12.0%), salaries (6.4%), port (4.0%) and maintenance (3.1%) [S15 note 22]. Coal prices reach PSAT through customer volumes and freight rates, not COGS, so the link is set to zero.

assumptions.label: Cost link 1: pass-through to prices
assumptions.basis: No coal-price cost exposure, so there is no cost to pass through; coal-cycle sensitivity is in the revenue line and the scenario revenue shocks [S15].

assumptions.label: Cost link 2: share of COGS exposed
assumptions.basis: Bunker fuel was Rp111.8bn of Rp931.0bn FY2025 cost of revenue, 12.0% [S15 note 22]; the tug, barge and bulk-carrier fleet burns marine fuel that moves with Brent. Depreciation is excluded because it is not a cash cost and is modelled separately.

assumptions.label: Cost link 2: pass-through to prices
assumptions.basis: Freight contracts reset periodically and pass most of a bunker move through: on the S14 build the H1 2026 cash gross margin was 40.7% (gross profit Rp82.9bn plus fixed and right-of-use depreciation Rp93.8bn on revenue Rp434.6bn), against 40.3% in H1 2025, although Brent averaged far higher, which shows the rate recovering most of the fuel increase [S14]. We leave a quarter of the move unpassed as a lag, not as a default squeeze.

assumptions.label: SG&A / revenue
assumptions.basis: FY2025 SG&A was Rp107.8bn, 10.0% of revenue; H1 2026 was Rp55.3bn on Rp434.6bn of revenue, 12.7%, as the fixed cost base met a smaller book [S15, S14]. FY2026E holds the H1 12.7%, and fades toward 10.8% as revenue recovers, the last-actual rate rather than an assumed efficiency gain.

assumptions.label: D&A / revenue
assumptions.basis: FY2025 total depreciation was Rp156.9bn, 14.6% of revenue (fixed assets Rp135.6bn plus right-of-use Rp21.3bn); H1 2026 ran at Rp93.8bn (fixed Rp82.9bn + right-of-use Rp10.9bn), annualising to about Rp188bn, 21.5% of FY2026E revenue, as the two bulk carriers bought with IPO proceeds entered service [S15, S14]. Absolute D&A is close to the fleet's replacement charge (vessels Rp1,429.4bn at 5-6%, docking Rp122.5bn at 40%), so the ratio falls only as revenue recovers toward the asset base; it does not fall because the charge is assumed away [S15 note 10].

assumptions.label: Capex / revenue
assumptions.basis: FY2025 capex was Rp442.2bn (41.1% of revenue), the year the company bought two bulk carriers with IPO proceeds and renewed the fleet; H1 2026 capex was Rp54.4bn (12.5% of H1 revenue) as the programme wound down [S15, S14]. Sustaining capex is anchored to the LK's own asset lives, not to D&A: vessels Rp1,429.4bn at 5-6% (Rp72-86bn), docking Rp122.5bn at 40% (Rp49bn) and other fixed assets about Rp22bn give Rp150-165bn of replacement spend, 17-19% of FY2026E revenue [S15 note 10]. Capex normalises from that replacement rate and holds at 17% of revenue, matching replacement rather than falling below D&A; a fleet growing 4% in perpetuity must be replaced, not run down.

assumptions.label: Operating working capital / revenue
assumptions.basis: FY2025 NWC was Rp303.0bn, 28.1% of revenue; at June 2026 it was Rp354.8bn against an annualised revenue base near Rp870bn, 40.8%, because contract assets and inventory rose while the book shrank [S15, S14]. We hold the June 2026 actual ratio of 40.8% through the forecast. There is no disclosed release or terms-of-trade improvement to support a fade, and the related-party goods book and inventory build point the other way, so no working-capital release is assumed.

assumptions.label: Effective tax rate
assumptions.basis: Tax is rebuilt from the LK, not carried at a flat 32%. Shipping revenue is taxed at a 1.20% FINAL rate (Rp9.10bn in FY2025) and only the non-shipping profit (shipyard, goods trading, interest, other) bears the 22% normal rate [S15 note 28]. Because the final levy is revenue-based, the effective rate is high when profit is thin and low when it recovers: 33.8% in FY2025 on Rp34.8bn of pretax, 7.1% in FY2024 on Rp262.1bn [S15 p18]. Modelling 1.2% on about 70% of revenue plus 22% on non-shipping pretax gives 23.1% in FY2026E falling to 14.6% long run; the engine carries the effective rate, so the FCFF charge is a revenue-linked levy rather than 32% of EBIT.

assumptions.label: Cost of debt (on opening debt)
assumptions.basis: FY2025 finance cost of Rp14.43bn on opening debt of Rp195.6bn, 7.4%, covering bank loans and lease interest [S15]; held at 7.5% for the forecast. The engine charges the rate on opening debt: FY2026E uses the December 2025 balance of Rp236.1bn even though the June 2026 debt is Rp175.2bn, so the FY2026E charge is marginally conservative and the charge falls from FY2027E on the repaid balance [S14].

assumptions.label: Yield on opening cash
assumptions.basis: FY2025 interest income of Rp1.33bn on opening cash of Rp183.0bn, 0.7%; the cash balance earns little [S15].

assumptions.label: Net new borrowing
assumptions.basis: The June 2026 balance sheet already shows debt down to Rp175.2bn from Rp236.1bn at December 2025, a net repayment of Rp60.9bn in H1 (bank loans Rp50.3bn plus lease payments Rp10.58bn) [S14], so we set FY2026E net borrowing to that actual and repay a further Rp10bn in FY2027; no new debt is added and the fleet programme is funded [S14].

assumptions.label: Other non-operating items
assumptions.basis: FY2025 other income net was Rp9.80bn, chiefly gains on vessel sales of Rp4.40bn and miscellaneous income [S15]. We carry Rp3.0bn fading to Rp2.0bn, excluding the one-off disposal gains.

assumptions.label: Minorities' share of net profit
assumptions.basis: The subsidiaries are effectively wholly owned; non-controlling interest is Rp2.9m on the balance sheet, so the minority share of profit is nil [S15].

assumptions.label: Dividend payout
assumptions.basis: The prospectus promises up to 100% of net profit from FY2026 [S10]; the board skipped the FY2025 dividend at the June 2026 AGM because the fleet programme was still being funded [S17], which is a capex decision on a prior fiscal year, not a policy for FY2026. With the fleet renewed and capex now at replacement, we model a 50% payout from FY2026 earnings, paid the following year: half of the stated ceiling, leaving headroom for the nickel/bauxite diversification. The FY2026 cash outflow is zero because FY2025 DPS was nil [S17]. The dividend-capacity table in the report shows DPS and FCFE yield at 25%, 50% and 100%.

assumptions.label: Change in share count
assumptions.basis: No rights issue or treasury programme is disclosed; the share count is held at the post-IPO 1,482.4m [S11].

assumptions.label: Terminal growth (DCF)
assumptions.basis: House terminal growth for a rupiah reporting currency; a domestic coal and nickel logistics operator delivers into a slowly growing fleet, so we use the standard rupiah rate rather than a coal-sector premium [S19].

challenges.challenge: Sustaining capex is 10% of revenue in FY2026E (Rp89.4bn) falling to 7.5% (Rp96.3bn in FY2035) while D&A is 18-20% (Rp178.8bn and Rp231.2bn) and the model grows 4% in perpetuity. The LK contradicts it: vessels cost Rp1,429.4bn at 5-6% p.a. (Rp72-86bn) plus docking stock Rp122.5bn at 40% (Rp49bn) implies replacement capex of Rp121-135bn, 13.5-15% of FY2026E revenue [S15 note 10], and H1 2026 capex alone was Rp54.4bn (12.5% of H1 revenue, annualising to Rp108.9bn), above the FY2026E input [S14]. With capex equal to D&A, FY2026E FCFF goes from +Rp70.8bn to -Rp18.6bn and FY2035 terminal FCFF from Rp157.7bn to Rp22.8bn, cutting the DCF towards Rp480/share. A 4% terminal growth with reinvestment below depreciation is not a going-concern steady state.
challenges.answer: Capex is now anchored to the LK's own asset lives, not to a revenue percentage: vessels of Rp1,429.4bn at 5-6%, docking assets of Rp122.5bn at 40% and the rest of the fixed-asset base give a replacement charge of about 17% of FY2026E revenue, held through FY2035E. The fleet no longer runs down to a fraction of book, and the DCF falls from the prior construction to Rp575/share. D&A was also re-based to the H1 2026 run-rate (fixed Rp82.9bn plus right-of-use Rp10.9bn, annualising to about 21.5% of FY2026E revenue, fading to 17% as revenue recovers).

challenges.challenge: The 29% expected return is not an operating case. The DCF is Rp854 against Rp845 (+1.0%), and v0 of Rp1,068 is 44% multiple-based (15% x Rp1,588 + 15% x Rp1,551 = Rp471 of Rp1,068). The weighted target needs the bull: at 25% probability the bull contributes Rp250 to the Rp1,361 weighted value and Rp200 of the Rp1,089 target; with the bull set equal to the base the target is Rp889 (+5.4%). The report calls the peer multiples 'very high or speculative' yet uses them for 30% of the blend, and the bull's 2pp WACC cut to 10.53% sits below every peer (ALII 12.52, BBRM 11.48) and rests only on a first dividend [S0].
challenges.answer: The bull WACC shock is cut from -2pp to -1pp (11.53%, above BBRM's 11.48% and no longer below every peer), mirrored by +1pp in the bear. The P/BV cross-check is dropped and the DCF weight raised to 85%, so the target no longer depends on multiple convergence. The report now states the DCF-only value (Rp575), the base-scenario target (Rp814) and the bull (Rp1,642) explicitly, and says that with the bull set equal to the base the weighted answer is the base case. The weighted target is Rp745, a -10.7% return, and the rating moves from BUY to REDUCE.

challenges.challenge: The H1 2026 revenue note shows the core owned fleet grew: third-party owned-to-freight revenue Rp252.5bn versus Rp217.8bn (+15.9%), total owned Rp254.7bn versus Rp217.8bn (+16.9%), while total revenue fell 20.4% [S14 note 22]. The decline is entirely the low-margin lines: re-charter Rp127.6bn vs Rp217.6bn (-41.4%), goods Rp48.9bn vs Rp92.1bn (-47.0%), docking Rp3.5bn vs Rp18.4bn (-81.2%). PSAT also outgrew the national quota cut (H1 revenue -20.4% against a 600Mt quota 26.6% below 2025 output). The report says only that revenue fell on a weaker coal cycle and never states that owned-vessel revenue rose 17%, so the FY2027E +4% and FY2028E +5% path assumes the core stalls.
challenges.answer: The revenue path is now built by line from the H1 2026 note: owned-vessel revenue of Rp254.7bn (Rp252.5bn third-party plus Rp2.2bn related) against Rp217.8bn, re-charter of Rp127.6bn against Rp217.6bn, goods of Rp48.9bn against Rp92.1bn and docking of Rp3.5bn against Rp18.4bn. FY2026E holds the H1 run-rate; FY2027E growth is raised from 4% to 6% on a 10% owned-fleet recovery with the re-charter and goods books flat. The owned-fleet growth is now stated in section 1 and 3 and carried in the bull narrative, and the thesis no longer says the core stalls.

challenges.challenge: The model's own FCFE yield reaches 9.97% by FY2028E (multiples table) on a 25% payout, and FY2028E net profit of Rp25.0bn would pay Rp16.8/share at the promised 100% payout. The report presents no dividend-capacity or FCFE-yield analysis, although the COAL_LOGISTICS card says the dividend is the market's anchor. The payout is set at 25% against the prospectus of up to 100% from FY2026 [S10] on the evidence of a skipped FY2025 dividend, which was a different fiscal year and a fleet-capex decision, not a FY2026 policy statement [S17].
challenges.answer: The payout is raised from 25% to 50% of net profit from FY2026, paid the following year, and the basis now treats the skipped FY2025 dividend as a fleet-capex decision on a prior year rather than a policy for FY2026. The report shows the capacity: FY2028E EPS of Rp42.0, DPS of Rp21.0 at the modelled half payout and the full EPS at the stated ceiling, an FCFE yield of 5.9% and a dividend yield of 2.5% against the prospectus of up to 100% of net profit.

challenges.challenge: FY2025's 9.9% revenue growth is entirely related-party: related-party revenue rose Rp97.3bn (Rp2.1bn to Rp99.4bn) while third-party revenue was flat (Rp978.1bn to Rp977.4bn) [S15 note 21]. Sales of goods were Rp226.0bn (21.0% of revenue), Rp86.3bn related-party and Rp139.7bn third-party, up 70% y/y from Rp133.0bn; the report calls this a larger third-party line without giving the total, gross margin, receivable or related-party share. Docking revenue fell 81% in H1 2026. This is the governance channel the report says it takes seriously and the revenue-quality question the H1 numbers raise.
challenges.answer: The goods line is now broken out: FY2025 sales of goods of Rp226.0bn (Rp86.3bn related-party plus Rp139.7bn third-party), a fifth of group revenue and more than a third related-party, up from Rp133.0bn; H1 2026 goods of Rp48.9bn (Rp35.9bn related plus Rp12.9bn third-party). The LK does not disclose the goods gross margin or a separate receivable balance, so the report says the margin is undisclosed rather than inventing one. FY2025 growth is restated as entirely related-party, with third-party revenue flat, and the June inventory build to Rp266.5bn is flagged as the related-party and liquidity channel. The counterparties are in the related-party note but are not named individually in a way that supports a per-counterparty split.

challenges.challenge: The revised 2026 RKAB of 700Mt is 117.48Mt (14.4%) below the 817.48Mt actually produced in 2025 [S23], and it is a quota target, not a miner-level allocation or a freight contract. The summary and section 2 frame the revision as 'restores cargoes', while the base assumes H2 2026 revenue of Rp459.2bn (+5.7% h/h) with no source for the October quota reaching PSAT's jetties before year-end; H1 revenue was -20.4% y/y [S14]. The risk table admits the 700 is below 2025, but the summary and bull narrative do not carry it.
challenges.answer: The summary and section 2 now state that the 700Mt revised quota is below the 817.48Mt actually produced in 2025 and is a national target, not a miner-level allocation or a PSAT freight contract. The unsourced second-half uplift is removed: FY2026E revenue holds H2 flat to H1, giving -19.3% on FY2025 rather than the prior -17%. No source supports a PSAT-specific October volume allocation, so the base does not assume one; the quota and nickel/bauxite contracts are in the bull narrative, and the risk table carries the gap.

challenges.challenge: cov_engine qc reports FY2026E EBITDA margin 22.97% versus FY2025A 18.11%, a 4.86pp gap 0.14pp below the 5pp BLOCK threshold, and there is no qc_justification. The decomposition is gross margin +2.46pp (13.54 to 16.0), D&A ratio +5.43pp (14.57 to 20.0) and opex ratio -1.99pp (10.01 to 12.0): the largest driver is the depreciation add-back, not the mix shift the report cites. Because EBITDA adds back D&A, a 5.4pp rise in the depreciation ratio mechanically lifts the margin even if the cash margin is unchanged.
